extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, scientists, students, and general readers interested in the philosophy, modeling, and applications of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for when and how mathematical operations and models should be applied, what counts as utility in mathematics (within mathematics and to other fields), and how to judge models' assumptions, purposes, and success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three aspects of addition
rubrics_metrics.description: Addition has three aspects: the algorithmic aspect (rules of manipulation), the formal laws that sums obey (e.g., a + b = b + a; (a + b) + c = a + (b + c); a + 1 > a), and the applications of addition (under what circumstances does one add?).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between knowing how to add (algorithm), knowing the formal laws, and knowing when it is appropriate to apply addition in real contexts; the third aspect (applications) is the hard one and is the source of many 'word problem' difficulties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of addition (context-sensitivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is and there can be no comprehensive systematization of all the situations in which it is appropriate to add; any systematic application of addition to a wide class of problems is done by fiat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether addition meaningfully represents the situation: e.g., grocery discounts, 'vector' pricing (price with multiple components), non-linear pricing of scarce goods, or social scoring schemes may render ordinary addition inappropriate or arbitrary. Deciding to 'go ahead and add' is often a convention whose reasonableness rests on past/future experience rather than on a priori rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of aggregated scores or 'figures of merit'
rubrics_metrics.description: Sums used as figures of merit (credit ratings, intelligence tests, demerit systems) are ad hoc aggregations that may not have clear interpretable meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question whether disparate components (criminal record vs salary, assorted test items) are commensurable and whether the final sum represents a meaningful quantity; recognize subjectivity in assigning partial credit and the ad hoc nature of point-addition systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical measurement and theory-dependence of addition
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical measures (e.g., mass, weight) are meaningful only within the context of a theory (e.g., Newtonian mechanics); additivity of mass is definitional within such a theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether naive arithmetic addition corresponds to the measured quantity given the governing physical theory and instrument calibration; beware of nonlinearities (e.g., spring response) and ensure calibration/definitions justify additive combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a mathematical model
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical model is 'any complete and consistent set of mathematical equations which are designed to correspond to some other entity, its prototype.' 'Equations' may be replaced by 'structure' if not numerical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or evaluating a model, ensure completeness and internal consistency and that the mathematical structure is intended to correspond to a specified prototype (physical, biological, social, psychological, conceptual, or even another model).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit statement of modeling hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Model-building requires the explicit proposal of hypotheses (H0, H1, …) about conservation laws, geometry, flow rates, perfect mixing, reaction order, instantaneous response, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List and examine assumptions explicitly; different sets of hypotheses produce different models (from the most general to simpler special cases). Evaluate which assumptions are defensible for the intended purpose and how they affect model complexity and solvability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of model complexity and strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: The art of modeling is adopting the proper strategy: choose between simpler models (fewer assumptions, tractable) and more general models (more assumptions, more equations) depending on the question at hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match model choice to the intended use (e.g., accurate short-term planetary positions vs questions of dynamical stability) and be aware that mathematical tractability and the nature of available solutions may constrain strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposes for which models are constructed
rubrics_metrics.description: Models may be constructed (1) to obtain answers about what will happen in the physical world, (2) to influence further experimentation or observation, (3) to foster conceptual progress and understanding, (4) to assist the axiomatization of the physical situation, (5) to foster mathematics and the art of making mathematical models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the intended purpose as an explicit criterion when evaluating a model: a model successful for conceptual understanding may be inadequate for predictive engineering tasks, and vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic acceptance of models (models-as-approximation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary practice often treats a model as a 'sometime thing,' a convenient approximation rather than an expression of eternal truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge models primarily on pragmatic criteria (usefulness, accuracy for intended scope) rather than claiming literal truth; be clear about domain of validity and limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion of success: empirical fit and explanatory depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Success of a theory or model is judged by how well it fits observations and by whether it provides deeper unifying explanations (contrast Ptolemaic curve-fitting vs Newtonian laws that introduce masses, accelerations, universal laws).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate both predictive accuracy and the model's ability to offer unifying, explanatory concepts; greater versatility and deeper vocabulary of mechanisms count as virtues even if empirical discrepancies remain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations from unknown forces/parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Models may require accounting for many possible forces and parameters (e.g., gravitational influences of many bodies); there is no systematic way a priori to know which forces are important—models become patchwork as new factors are added.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be modest about claims of completeness; treat models as subject to revision when new influential factors are discovered and assess sensitivity to neglected forces/parameters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model evaluation vis-à-vis computational/mathematical limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be a gap between what we want a theory to do and what the available mathematics can accomplish; this controls subsequent methodology and choice of model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select modeling approaches cognizant of mathematical solvability/numerical feasibility. For some questions use analytic solutions; for others accept approximation/numerical simulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility of mathematics to mathematics (pure application criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A piece of mathematics is 'used' in another part of mathematics when its materials, structure, techniques, or insights are used to cast light on or derive inferences about the other; historically the direction of influence can reverse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate internal (pure) utility by tracing whether methods or theorems materially contribute to results in other mathematical domains; note that 'utility' can change with time and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of theorems by utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between a useful theorem (an application has been found), a very useful theorem (many applications), and a useless theorem (no application found thus far).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging mathematical work, consider how many nontrivial applications are known and resist artificially splicing additional conditions to force applications (such tricks violate aesthetic standards). Recognize that utility judgments may be historical and evolve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility to other scientific or technological fields (applied mathematics evaluation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applied mathematics must be evaluated by how it connects to other disciplines, whether intermediate theories (e.g., elasticity) then connect to practical engineering, and ultimately whether it affects outcomes at the level of the man in the street.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace application chains from abstract math → disciplinary theory → engineering practice → consumer impact. Evaluations should be specific and documented rather than vague claims of potential applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common utility (end-to-end applicability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common utility is the extension of mathematical application all the way to the man in the street (consumer-level benefits); this is a distinct and important standard of utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use common-utility as a rigorous test when appropriate: does the mathematics lead to measurable, practical improvements in everyday contexts? Be cautious in claiming common utility without concrete evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Barriers to achieving common utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential mathematical applications may be blocked because they are too difficult, too expensive, too inaccurate, require unavailable parameters, or because alternative testing is cheaper/more reliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating an applied mathematical proposal, analyze feasibility, cost-benefit, parameter availability, accuracy, and whether empirical testing might be a superior route to the desired practical outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pure vs applied value tensions (aesthetic vs practical criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a tension in valuing mathematics: some (Hardyism) prize elegance and 'useless' beauty above practical use, while others (Mathematical Maoism) demand socially useful research; attitudes affect teaching, research, and career incentives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge differing value systems when assessing mathematical work; evaluation frameworks should state whether priority is given to elegance/profundity or to utility and practical impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model social consequences and institutional inertia
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a mathematical system (tax computation, welfare formulas, numbering systems) is established 'by fiat' it carries social consequences and institutional back-up that make it hard to remove without disruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the broader social, administrative, and institutional impacts when designing or recommending mathematical systems; anticipate lock-in and political/operational resistance to change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ad hoc nature of scoring systems and the need for interpretability
rubrics_metrics.description: Many institutional scoring systems (bank credit points, test aggregates) are ad hoc; partial credit is often subjective and the relation between items and what is being measured can be unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand clarity about the construct being measured, transparency in how component scores combine, and empirical validation of the aggregated score's meaning before relying on such systems for decisions.
